sources.headline: Anti-government protesters battle with police in Albania
sources.text: Figure caption, Watch: The BBC reports from Tirana, where violent protests grew on SaturdayByNick ThorpeCorrespondentReporting fromTirana, AlbaniaDemonstrators and riot police fought pitched battles in the centre of Tirana on Saturday for the fifth day in a row. Masked protesters, many of them high school and university students, hurled rocks and petrol bombs at riot police trying to defend the education ministry, one of the focal points of the protests. The police responded with water cannon and volleys of tear gas, sending the crowds scattering. There are also reports that rubber bullets were used for the first time.Protests which began in the summer have grown into a wider anti-government movement, with calls for the prime minister to resign following corruption allegations linked to his administration.Many of the protesters in central Tirana wore gas masks or face masks, while volunteers handed out syringes of saline eyewash to reduce the pain from the tear gas which billows down the street.The constant boom of petrol bombs could be heard exploding on Saturday.During the afternoon, the focus of the protests shifted to the office of Prime Minister Edi Rama on the city's main boulevard. Here the crowds swelled to far larger numbers than on previous days. Riot police faced a steady hail of cobble stones and fireworks, and responded with barrage after barrage of tear gas, some of the canisters landing far back in the crowds, causing panic. Incensed by the gas, the crowds waited for it to clear, then renewed their attacks.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Demonstrators come equipped to clean tear gas from people's eyesBlack smoke from a burning vehicle and the sirens of police cars and ambulances split the afternoon. As dusk fell, police special forces arrived to reinforce the riot police. Many people have been injured on both sides, 80 people have been charged with disorder so far, and hundreds more have been arrested, or are under investigation.The centre of the Tirana looks increasingly like a war zone, scattered with broken glass and burnt debris.George, a 19-year-old medical student who works as an electrician to fund his studies, stood near the burnt-out education ministry building, a scarf wrapped round his face and goggles covering his eyes. He is one of the thousands who have taken part in the increasingly intense protests which began in early June.In his gloved hands he clutched two rocks intended for the police.Asked if he was concerned about injuring them, he said: "We have mothers too. We have family too."We were peaceful for 135 days. Now we are trying to do like in France… we are trying to make a revolution. "Our government doesn't want peace, so we are using violence."Image caption, Klodi, 21 and Klea, 17, were among the young student protesters in Tirana on Saturday Many of the protesters were even younger. Klea, 17, is in her first year of university in Tirana. She said: "All the students are boycotting their university classes and left school to fight for our rights." She alleged there were provocateurs among the protesters, smashing up stores and banks, to discredit the demonstrations.Image caption, Protesters and riot police fought running battles throughout the day in the centre of the capital Socialist Party Prime Minister Edi Rama has been in power for 13 years and has dominated Albanian politics, much like his main rival Sali Berisha, of the opposition Democratic Party, did for decades. The students say they are against "the whole corrupt political class". So what is the alternative?Osman Stafa, a prominent journalist for the News24 channel, who also describes himself as an activist for change, called for a "neutral, caretaker government for one year, to organise new elections".The irony for the wider European community during this latest wave of unrest is that Rama has long been viewed favourably by the EU, which Albania aspires to join.In a social media post on Saturday morning, he urged Albanian to "not forget that we have achieved extraordinary things".He blamed the protests on the opposition Democratic Party, and on what he called "the sinister agenda of foreign actors, intent on halting our progress" towards EU membership, which he has promised by 2030. He did not name which "foreign actors" he had in mind.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Protesters threw bricks at police on the city's main boulevard The latest protests have seriously tarnished Rama's carefully cultivated image as a charming leader, steering his country towards prosperity. Parallel to the protests, a series of investigations by the special prosecution service also threaten his rule. Set up under EU and US pressure in 2019, the prosecutors recently arrested the powerful secret service chief Vlora Hyseni. She stands accused of helping a prominent businessman, former government official, and personal friend of Rama, Ergys Agasi, evade justice. The 39-year-old is under arrest. Agasi, speaking through his lawyer, denied the allegations against him and said he had nothing to do with corruption. Hyseni told prosecutors that she contacted Agasi to try to recruit him to the intelligence services, Albanian media reported.Several Albanian media outlets claim he acted as an intermediary between the prime minister and organised criminal groups. Rama has admitted that he knows Agasi but denies any knowledge of illegal transactions."Edi Rama is caught between a rock and a hard place," Lutfi Dervishi, a political analyst and university lecturer, told the BBC. "He's the victim of his own success. By concentrating so much power in his own hands, he has made himself the only person the people blame for their grievances."Rama's Socialist Party has a comfortable majority, with 83 out of 140 seats in the Albanian Parliament. The next parliamentary elections are not due till 2029.

sources.headline: Violent protests a threat to EU membership, not government, Albanian PM says
sources.text: Albania's prime minister has said he will not resign despite days of protest and growing unrest, warning that the escalating violence is threatening the country's chances of joining the European Union.

sources.headline: Albanian PM says protests pose threat to EU membership, not government
sources.text: TIRANA - Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama on Oct 18 rejected calls to step down and said street protests, which continued for a sixth day, were a threat not to his government but to Albania’s hopes of joining the European Union.Student-led demonstrations, fuelled by anger over perceived government corruption, a lack of jobs and poor education standards, have engulfed central Tirana and spread to other cities in the past week.Demonstrators demanding Rama’s resignation have set fire to government buildings as well as banks, smashed shop windows and pulled up paving stones to throw at police.Violence erupted again on Oct 18 when thousands gathered outside the Education Ministry and hurled rocks at riot police who responded with tear gas, water cannon and rubber bullets.The unrest, which followed months of largely peaceful protests over the summer against a luxury coastal development backed by US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, pose the biggest challenge yet to Rama, who has governed since 2013 and in 2025 won a fourth term in office.“I am not being challenged, the government is not being challenged, a government majority or a winning party in the elections is not being challenged but a path is being challenged, a mission is being challenged,” Rama said in a live address on Facebook.“Albanians need to think very clearly: Do they want this, do they want that, or do they want the EU?”Rama invited students to dialogue as excavators dug up and removed the paving outside his office in central Tirana before protests started on Oct 18.The US embassy in Tirana urged protesters to refrain from violence.“Violence, rioting, physically injuring others, and the destruction of property are not civic engagement,” it said on X.Corruption scandals have tarnished Albania’s image over the years and analysts say the country is a hub for gangs seeking to launder money from drugs and weapons trafficking.However, Rama has said his government is tackling corruption as never before.Along with Montenegro, Albania is currently leading the posse of Balkan countries seeking to join the EU, and is aiming for entry by 2030.Rama blamed unspecified foreign interests for the protests and for what he said was an attempted drone attack at his office this week.“God knows what the consequences will be. There are no young people, no students, and no minors who would even think of implementing this plan. This is a foreign hand,” he said.Police said 388 people had been charged with criminal offences during the demonstrations.Scores of police officers and protesters have been injured. REUTERS

sources.headline: Student protests in Albania turn violent as demonstrators clash with police
sources.text: Tens of thousands of students have taken to the streets of Tirana, the Albanian capital, setting alight a government building and two banks and hurling stones at police during a protest over rising education costs and ⁠corruption.Police responded with water ⁠cannon and teargas to disperse protesters who started a fire at the ministry of education building, overturned bins and smashed the fronts of local businesses. A branch of Raiffeisen Bank near the education ministry also caught fire.Authorities said 23 police officers and six other people were being treated for injuries and that 35 people had been detained.President Bajram Begaj condemned the violence and appealed for calm, adding: “The constitution and the law must remain the boundaries for everyone, without exception.”The protests are the most violent outburst yet against Edi Rama, ⁠the prime minister, who won a fourth term in office in May last year but has since faced ​growing discontent at perceived graft surrounding top ‌officials. Protesters also dismiss opposition figures ‌as unpalatable alternatives.Protesters clash with police in central Tirana. Photograph: Adnan Beci/AFP/GettyThe unrest caps a summer of peaceful protests against Rama, triggered by the proposed development ‌of a luxury resort along Albania’s pristine southern coast backed by Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, which has been caught up in legal disputes.“This is a revolution. We are tired of peaceful protests. We will not stop until Rama resigns,” said Lora, a student who declined to give her last name as she threw rocks at the police.Others chanted “resignation” and “police of crime”.Student ‌organisers said the protest was over conditions at universities, higher education costs, a lack of financial support and employment prospects after graduation.The unrest is part of a ​broader wave of student activism sweeping Europe over education and living conditions. In France, high school students have staged weeks of protests and school blockades demanding more teachers and better facilities, arguing that deteriorating school buildings and overcrowded classrooms are undermining education.Albanian media reported that Wednesday’s protests had spread to universities at Elbasan and Shkodër.The government ⁠condemned the violence.skip past newsletter promotionafter newsletter promotionA government building and two banks were set on fire during the protests. Photograph: Florion Goga/ReutersAlbana Koçiu, the deputy prime minister of Albania, said on Facebook: “Protesting is a legitimate right, but it cannot be used ​as an excuse for violence, city ​destruction or ugly fighting in the middle ​of the road. I call on ​students and every ‌honest citizen who believes in ​the right to ​protest: distance yourself from violence and vandalism!”The police issued a statement calling for calm. “Any person who uses violence, burns or destroys property, or attacks police officers, bears individual responsibility and will face the law, in accordance with the offences committed,” they said.Meanwhile, the EU, which the Balkan nation aspires to join, voiced concern over what it called the “violent escalation at the protest in Tirana”.A statement by the EU delegation in Tirana said: “We take note of the allegations of excessive violence by the police against protesters and journalists,”Calling for a prompt investigation, the delegation encouraged “all sides to de-escalate the tension”.

sources.headline: Albania: Fire at Education Ministry as students protest
sources.text:
Albania's Education Ministry caught fire on Wednesday in a second day of student protests over corruption and education.
The scenes were at least somewhat reminiscent of the protracted student demonstrations in France in recent weeks.
They are probably the most violent outburst of low-level anti-corruption protests against Prime Minister Edi Rama's government and the main opposition led by Sali Barisha that started in May this year.
Many of the demonstrators wore face coveringsImage: Florion Goga/REUTERS
What happened in Tirana's student protests?
Police deployed riot police and used tear gas and water cannons to disperse crowds in the capital Tirana. Thousands of protesters gathered in front of the Education Ministry on Wednesday, many obscuring their faces. Some threw bricks at the building, damaged barriers on the sidewalks and overturned trash cans.
A bank near the Education Ministry also caught fire, according to the Reuters news agency citing a witness.
The demonstration started on Tuesday with a peaceful gathering of several hundred people outside the Education Ministry but quickly escalated and turned violent in places.
Police early on Wednesday reported around 40 detentions and 13 people injured, including six police officers. Unrest continued long after these figures were issued.
Police used tear gas and water cannons on demonstrators in parts of TiranaImage: Florion Goga/REUTERS
Government says demonstrations degenerated into 'orchestrated violence'
Deputy Prime Minster Albana Kociu posted a video of demonstrations on Facebook saying it was "disheartening to see the culture of protest degenerate into orchestrated violence."
She said that the attacks on institutions and police and the "senseless destruction of public property" were "not the language through which the youth should express themselves." Instead, she said they were reminiscent of the "old habits of those who use young people to mask their own political incompetence."
In another post, Kociu called on students who believe in the right to protest to "distance" themselves from "violence and vandalism."
Student organizers say the protests revolve around conditions at universities, higher education costs, financial support and employment prospects after graduation.
More generally, Albania has faced a series of demonstrations this year sometimes referred to as the "Flamingo Revolution." These were at least partly prompted by a controversial construction project on the Adriatic Coast in a protected area where flamingos live.
But these partly environmental protests have also had a more general theme of dissatisfaction with Albania's dominant political forces. PM Edi Rama's Socialists and Sali Barisha's right-wing Democrats have alternated in government for more than 30 years, ever since the post-Cold War democratic transition in the former communist country. Albania: Europe's new billionaire playgroundTo view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
The timing is also conspicuous, with the demonstrations starting amid prominent international coverage of widespread school and student protests in France in recent weeks leading to similarly restless scenes.
Edited by: Wesley Dockery
